hook: Badrinarayanan helped write one of computer vision's most-cited deep learning papers, SegNet, before moving into frontier AI research at DeepMind, and now leads AI development at Wayve, applying end-to-end learned driving models rather than the hand-coded rule systems most autonomous vehicle companies rely on.
name: Vijay Badrinarayanan

quote.text: The future of autonomous driving is not thousands of hand-coded rules, it's a single AI system that learns to drive the way humans do, from experience.
quote.context: A recurring theme in Badrinarayanan's public remarks on Wayve's end-to-end learning approach

moniker: Computer Vision Researcher Behind SegNet and Wayve's Self-Driving AI

reading.body:
Vijay Badrinarayanan's career traces a path from foundational perception research to one of the highest-stakes applications of that research: replacing hand-engineered autonomous vehicle pipelines with a single learned system trained end-to-end from sensor input.

SegNet, published in 2015, introduced an encoder-decoder architecture for pixel-wise image segmentation that became a standard reference across computer vision research and industry. That work sits at the base of the perception stack that autonomous driving depends on, because a vehicle that cannot reliably parse a scene cannot act on it. The move to DeepMind in 2016 extended that foundation into broader deep learning research before a focused return to applied perception at Wayve in 2021. The through-line is consistent: how machines extract structured meaning from raw visual data.

The distinction Badrinarayanan draws at Wayve, between thousands of hand-coded rules and a single system that learns from experience, is a design philosophy choice with real compute consequences. End-to-end learned models shift the burden from engineering labor to training compute and data, which means the approach's viability scales with available hardware and the volume of driving experience that can be collected and processed. The data here covers his published contributions and roles but does not address training infrastructure, fleet size, or how Wayve's compute requirements compare to rule-based competitors, so the full cost structure of the end-to-end bet remains outside what this record can support.
